analysis.investment_thesis: Arvind Limited trades at INR 387 — approximately 80% above its Graham Number of ~INR 215 (sqrt(22.5 × EPS₁₄ × BVPS₁₄₆)) — with a P/E of 24.1x and P/B of 2.64x, both far exceeding my strict thresholds of 15x and 1.5x respectively. A 9-year revenue CAGR of just 0.4% and a net loss in FY2021 disqualify this from meeting my requirement of consistent, proven earning power.
key_strengths: Debt deleveraging is genuine — borrowings fell from INR 2,640 Cr (2020) to INR 1,537 Cr (2025), with D/E a comfortable 0.39x
Operating cash flow positive in all 5 measured years — the business is not a cash incinerator
Gross margin of 49% suggests reasonable pricing power in its fabric segments
key_risks: Price trades at 80% premium to Graham Number (~INR 215 vs market INR 387) — no margin of safety whatsoever
Net loss in FY2021 (-INR 27 Cr) breaks the consecutive-earnings requirement; revenue CAGR over 9 years is a negligible 0.4%
FCF collapsed from INR 687 Cr (2021) to INR 280 Cr (2025) as capex surged to INR 535 Cr — capital allocation risk rising
red_flags: P/B of 2.64x — well above my 2.0x red-flag threshold; paying a large premium for assets in a commodity textile business
FY2021 net loss violates multi-year positive earnings rule — earnings are fragile, not durable
EBITDA CAGR of -3.1% over 9 years means the business has not compounded in real terms — a fundamental test of business quality that it fails
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Applying my quantitative filters, Arvind fails on nearly every count. The Graham Number computes to approximately INR 215 (using FY2025 EPS of ~INR 14 and BVPS of ~INR 146 on ~26.2 Cr shares), yet Mr. Market prices it at INR 387 — an 80% premium with zero margin of safety. P/E at 24.1x is 60% above my ceiling of 15x, and P/B at 2.64x is nearly double my preferred level of 1.5x. These are not numbers that offer the defensive investor any protection. The business has been essentially treading water for a decade: revenue grew at just 0.4% annually from 2016 to 2025, and EBITDA actually shrank at -3.1% per year. A company that cannot grow its earning power over nine years does not merit a premium valuation.

The balance sheet shows genuine improvement — debt has been cut meaningfully and D/E of 0.39x passes my leverage test — and operating cash flow has remained positive throughout. These are not nothing. But a sound balance sheet cannot rescue a stock trading at 80% above intrinsic value. The accelerating capex (INR 535 Cr in FY2025 vs INR 186 Cr in FY2022) is compressing free cash flow precisely at a time when returns on existing capital (ROE 9.3%, ROCE 13%) are already mediocre. The intelligent investor demands a discount to proven value, not a premium to speculative improvement. Arvind today offers neither the price nor the earnings quality to warrant purchase.
